name: The example
expr: (lambda p: (lambda r: (lambda ok: [ok, (p[r[0]][0] - p[r[1]][0]) ** 2 + (p[r[0]][1] - p[r[1]][1]) ** 2 if ok else None])(len(r) == 2 and all(isinstance(i, int) and 0 <= i < len(p) for i in r) and r[0] != r[1]))(tuple(closest_pair(list(p)))))(args[0])
show: closest_pair(the 12 points of the lesson's figure): [two different positions?, their squared distance]
why: [True, 2]: positions 5 and 6, the points (7, 3) and (8, 4), one on each side of the middle. Each half's best pair is further apart (8 and 5), so the strip around the dividing line is needed.

name: The same point twice
expr: (lambda p: (lambda r: (lambda ok: [ok, (p[r[0]][0] - p[r[1]][0]) ** 2 + (p[r[0]][1] - p[r[1]][1]) ** 2 if ok else None])(len(r) == 2 and all(isinstance(i, int) and 0 <= i < len(p) for i in r) and r[0] != r[1]))(tuple(closest_pair(list(p)))))(args[0])
show: closest_pair([(1, 1), (5, 5), (1, 1)]): [two different positions?, their squared distance]
why: [True, 0]: positions 0 and 2 hold the same point, so their distance is 0. Return two different positions, not the same one twice.

name: On a horizontal line
expr: (lambda p: (lambda r: (lambda ok: [ok, (p[r[0]][0] - p[r[1]][0]) ** 2 + (p[r[0]][1] - p[r[1]][1]) ** 2 if ok else None])(len(r) == 2 and all(isinstance(i, int) and 0 <= i < len(p) for i in r) and r[0] != r[1]))(tuple(closest_pair(list(p)))))(args[0])
show: closest_pair([(0, 0), (10, 0), (3, 0), (7, 0)]): [two different positions?, their squared distance]
why: [True, 9]: (0, 0) and (3, 0), or (7, 0) and (10, 0). Either pair is accepted.

name: Negative coordinates
expr: (lambda p: (lambda r: (lambda ok: [ok, (p[r[0]][0] - p[r[1]][0]) ** 2 + (p[r[0]][1] - p[r[1]][1]) ** 2 if ok else None])(len(r) == 2 and all(isinstance(i, int) and 0 <= i < len(p) for i in r) and r[0] != r[1]))(tuple(closest_pair(list(p)))))(args[0])
show: closest_pair([(-5, -5), (4, 4), (-2, -1), (3, 9), (-3, -3)]): [two different positions?, their squared distance]
why: [True, 5]: (-2, -1) and (-3, -3). Square the differences; do not take absolute values of the coordinates.

name: Across the middle
expr: (lambda p: (lambda r: (lambda ok: [ok, (p[r[0]][0] - p[r[1]][0]) ** 2 + (p[r[0]][1] - p[r[1]][1]) ** 2 if ok else None])(len(r) == 2 and all(isinstance(i, int) and 0 <= i < len(p) for i in r) and r[0] != r[1]))(tuple(closest_pair(list(p)))))(args[0])
show: closest_pair([(0, 0), (0, 10), (0, 20), (9, 5), (10, 5), (19, 0), (19, 10), (19, 20)]): [two different positions?, their squared distance]
why: [True, 1]: (9, 5) and (10, 5) end up in different halves. A method that only solves the two halves misses them.

name: A grid and one more point
args: ([(3 * i, 3 * j) for i in range(30) for j in range(30)] + [(44, 46)],)
expr: (lambda p: (lambda r: (lambda ok: [ok, (p[r[0]][0] - p[r[1]][0]) ** 2 + (p[r[0]][1] - p[r[1]][1]) ** 2 if ok else None])(len(r) == 2 and all(isinstance(i, int) and 0 <= i < len(p) for i in r) and r[0] != r[1]))(tuple(closest_pair(list(p)))))(args[0])
show: closest_pair(a 30 × 30 grid with gaps of 3, plus (44, 46)): [two different positions?, their squared distance]
why: [True, 2]: (44, 46) is 1 across and 1 up from (45, 45). Every grid pair is 9 apart, and there are many ties among them.

name: 40,000 scattered points
expr: (lambda p: (lambda r: (lambda ok: [ok, (p[r[0]][0] - p[r[1]][0]) ** 2 + (p[r[0]][1] - p[r[1]][1]) ** 2 if ok else None])(len(r) == 2 and all(isinstance(i, int) and 0 <= i < len(p) for i in r) and r[0] != r[1]))(tuple(closest_pair(list(p)))))(args[0])
show: closest_pair(40,000 points in a 1,000,000 square): [two different positions?, their squared distance]
why: Checking all pairs is 800 million distances. Divide and conquer with the strip is O(n log n).

name: 30,000 points on a vertical line
expr: (lambda p: (lambda r: (lambda ok: [ok, (p[r[0]][0] - p[r[1]][0]) ** 2 + (p[r[0]][1] - p[r[1]][1]) ** 2 if ok else None])(len(r) == 2 and all(isinstance(i, int) and 0 <= i < len(p) for i in r) and r[0] != r[1]))(tuple(closest_pair(list(p)))))(args[0])
show: closest_pair(30,000 points that all have x = 0): [two different positions?, their squared distance]
why: A sweep that sorts by x and compares each point with the following ones while their x is close never stops early here, because every x is the same: O(n²). The strip, sorted by y, with at most 7 comparisons per point, stays O(n log n).
